As an Android user, these are the first 5 settings I changed on the iPhone 18 Pro

An Apple with a Pixel complex.

•

•

•

Android and iOS couldn’t be more different, and I was reminded of that the moment I switched from my Pixel 11 Pro XL to the iPhone 18 Pro. I’d spent so much time on Android that I had almost forgotten how different things work on an iPhone. And believe me, the first day was quite an adjustment. I kept trying to swipe back from the right edge of the screen, only to remember that iOS doesn’t support Android’s universal back gesture.

Of course, I knew switching to an iPhone would mean giving up some of the things I’d grown accustomed to on Android. But that didn’t mean I had to leave every familiar habit behind. So, before I could properly settle into using the iPhone 18 Pro, I started exploring its settings to see how much of my Android experience I could bring over. A few changes later, my iPhone started feeling much more familiar, and these settings made the biggest difference.

0 votes

Green bubbles deserve some love, too

Shimul Sood / Android Authority

The first thing I did after setting up my iPhone 18 Pro was to enable RCS messaging. Most of my conversations happen through the Messages app, and since quite a few of my friends use Android phones, I didn’t want texting them to feel like a downgrade. With regular SMS, you miss things I’ve grown used to on Android, like read receipts, typing indicators, and sharing high-quality photos and videos.

iPhones now support RCS, which makes texting Android users much better. This makes switching between Android and iPhone feel less inconvenient, especially since I message throughout the day. If you want to enable RCS on your iPhone, here’s how:

1. Open the Settings app on your iPhone.

2. Scroll down to Apps and select Messages.

3. Under Text Messaging, tap RCS Messaging.

4. Toggle on RCS Messaging to send and receive supported messages over Wi-Fi or mobile data.

And that’s all it takes. It might seem like a small change, but it made texting my Android friends feel just as familiar as it did on my Pixel, which was exactly what I wanted.

One notification at a time, please

Shimul Sood / Android Authority

Next, I wanted my iPhone notifications to feel a little more like Android. By default, iOS groups notifications into a stack, which looks neat, but I’ve never really been a fan. After spending so much time with Android’s notification shade, where I can quickly scroll through my alerts and see what’s happening, having everything piled on top of each other felt a little strange.

By default, iOS groups notifications into a stack, which looks neat, but I've never really been a fan.

Thankfully, Apple lets you change how notifications appear on your lock screen, and switching to the List view made things feel much more familiar. Here’s how you can do it, too:

1. Open the Settings app on your iPhone.

2. Scroll down and tap Notifications.

3. Under Display As, select List instead of Stack.

And that’s all there is to it. Your notifications will now appear in a list on the Lock Screen, making it easier to scroll through them without expanding a stack first. It doesn’t completely recreate Android’s notification shade, but it’s much closer to what I’m used to, and that’s good enough for me.

Apple’s defaults aren’t my defaults

Shimul Sood / Android Authority

Another thing I wanted to sort out was the default apps on my iPhone. One thing I love about Android is being able to choose which apps I want to use for pretty much everything. And while Apple has its own apps for browsing, emailing, and other tasks, I didn’t necessarily want to start using all of them just because I’d switched to an iPhone.

For instance, I’ve used Chrome as my primary browser and Gmail for emails for years, so switching to Safari and Apple Mail would just mean getting used to another set of apps. Thankfully, iOS lets you change several default apps, which means I could bring some of my familiar Android setup straight to my iPhone 18 Pro. I replaced Safari with Chrome, switched from Apple Mail to Gmail, and explored the other options to see what else I could customize.

If you want to do the same, here’s how:

1. Open Settings on your iPhone and go to Apps.

2. Tap Default Apps at the top.

3. You’ll see different categories, including Email, Messaging, Calling, Browser App, and Call Filtering, among others.

4. Open each category and select the app you’d prefer to use, as long as it’s installed and supports being set as the default.

Once I’d made these changes, I no longer had to think about which app would open whenever I tapped a link or an email address. My iPhone started using the apps I was already comfortable with, which made the transition from Android much easier.

80% is the sweet spot

Shimul Sood / Android Authority

One feature I didn’t want to leave behind on my Pixel 11 Pro XL was the 80% charging limit. I’ve been using it for quite some time now, mainly because I want to keep my phone’s battery in good shape for as long as possible. I don’t always need a full charge to get through the day, so limiting it to 80% feels like a reasonable trade-off if it helps reduce battery wear in the long run.

Apple offers a similar feature on the iPhone 18 Pro, so I didn’t have to change my charging habits after switching. In fact, setting it up was just as easy as it was on my Pixel. Here’s how you can enable it:

1. Open the Settings app on your iPhone.

2. Scroll down and tap Battery.

3. Select Charging.

4. Adjust the Charge Limit slider to 80% instead of 100%.

And that’s all there is to it. Your iPhone will now generally stop charging at 80%, although it may occasionally charge to 100% to maintain accurate battery-level estimates. Keeping the limit at 80% can help reduce battery wear over time, especially if you tend to leave your phone plugged in for long periods.

Keeping the lights low, Pixel-style

Shimul Sood / Android Authority

Finally, I wanted the Always-On Display on my iPhone 18 Pro to look a little more like the one on my Pixel 11 Pro XL. I’ve always preferred Google’s approach to the Always-On Display: a clean, black background with only the essential information visible. Apple’s version, on the other hand, feels a little too busy for my liking, especially with the wallpaper and notifications showing up even when the phone is locked.

Apple lets you customize what appears on the Always-On Display, and turning off just two options made a big difference.

Thankfully, I didn’t have to live with that. Apple lets you customize what appears on the Always-On Display, and turning off just two options made a big difference. Here’s how you can do the same:

1. Open the Settings app on your iPhone.

2. Scroll down and select Display & Brightness.

3. Tap Always On Display.

4. Turn off Show Wallpaper and Show Notifications.

My iPhone 18 Pro now has a much cleaner, mostly black Always-On Display, with the clock and other essential information still visible. It’s much closer to the minimal look I loved on my Pixel, and my wallpaper no longer lights up the screen every time I glance at my phone.

You can take me out of Android, but…

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

These changes helped me feel more at home on my iPhone 18 Pro. Now, you might be wondering why I’d switch to an iPhone only to make it behave more like an Android phone. Fair question. I really wanted to experience what Apple has to offer without giving up everything I’ve grown accustomed to over the years.

I’m still exploring iOS and getting used to how things work differently, which is part of the fun of testing a new phone. At the same time, I don’t see why I should force myself to change habits that already work perfectly well for me, especially when Apple lets me keep them.

So, if you’re considering moving from Android to iPhone, I’d recommend trying these changes. They won’t solve every frustration or make iOS behave exactly like Android, but they’ll certainly make those first few days feel less unfamiliar. Switching phones should be about enjoying something new, not constantly wishing you still had your old one.

Anker’s most powerful portable charger just hit a new low. The Anker Prime 26,250mAh power bank with its Fast Charging Base is down to $229.99 on Amazon, which is $100 off its $329.99 list price and $30 below the deal we covered in September.

This is a power bank built for people who carry a lot of gear. The Anker Prime delivers up to 300W of total output and can power up to six devices at once when docked on its base, so a laptop, phone, tablet, and earbuds can all charge together.

The 300W output is enough to fast charge a MacBook alongside your phone, which makes it a good fit for creators, photographers, and anyone working away from a desk. Two-way fast charging means the power bank itself refills quickly too, especially when you drop it onto the included charging base.

Anker’s app lets you check battery levels and manage charging from your phone, and the 26,250mAh capacity is designed to be flight-safe, so you can take it in your carry-on.

The deal comes from a third-party seller, but the order ships from Amazon. Shoppers rate it 4.6 out of five stars.

At $229.99, the Anker Prime power bank is still a premium buy, but this is the cheapest it has ever been.

XREAL AURA review: Is Android XR really worth it?

The XREAL AURA is easily the best Android XR system you can buy today — if you actually need Android XR.

•

XREAL AURA

It's a pricey investment and Google's operating system hasn't reach its full potential yet, but the XREAL AURA arguably offers the best Android XR experience to date by shrinking nearly everything impressive about the Samsung Galaxy XR into a comfortable pair of tethered glasses and a pocket-sized compute puck.

Comfortable for long sessions

Flexible control options

What we don't like

No power brick or display-mirroring cable in box

XREAL AURA

It's a pricey investment and Google's operating system hasn't reach its full potential yet, but the XREAL AURA arguably offers the best Android XR experience to date by shrinking nearly everything impressive about the Samsung Galaxy XR into a comfortable pair of tethered glasses and a pocket-sized compute puck.

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

Notable for being among the first AR glasses to run Google’s relatively new Android XR operating system, the XREAL AURA aim to solve the biggest problem with mixed-reality headsets: bulk. The easiest way to describe the XREAL AURA is as a slimmed-down version of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR headset — split into a pair of glasses, a cable, and a compute puck.

After spending real time with the XREAL AURA (provided to me by XREAL for review), I came away genuinely impressed by the hardware. In fact, I struggled to find much wrong with the glasses themselves. The problem isn’t what XREAL built — it’s figuring out whether Android XR is actually worth paying a premium for.

A shrunk-down Galaxy XR

C. Scott Brown / Android Authority

To keep the eyewear light on your face, XREAL offloads all the Android XR compute and battery hardware into a separate tethered puck. The puck is roughly the same footprint as my Google Pixel 11 Pro, though it’s noticeably heavier at 265g.

Inside that puck is serious silicon: the Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset (which debuted in June 2026 and is currently Qualcomm’s most powerful XR chip), paired with 12GB or 16GB of RAM, up to 512GB of UFS 4.0 storage, and a 4,455mAh battery. The glasses themselves weigh 95g, and house XREAL’s X1S spatial coprocessor alongside dual Sony Micro-OLED displays (1,920 x 1,200 per eye, up to 120Hz) using X Prism optics with a 70-degree field of view.

Because the puck packs flagship XR horsepower into a small chassis, it has an active cooling fan built in. It needs it, too: under heavy load, the puck can get pretty toasty. Thankfully, XREAL anticipates this and includes a belt clip right in the retail box. Snapping the clip onto the puck and hanging it from your belt is far more comfortable than keeping a tiny furnace in your pants pocket.

C. Scott Brown / Android Authority

In fact, XREAL gives you a generous bundle out of the box. You get a terrific hard carrying case that neatly holds both the glasses and the puck, complete with an upper pouch for cables. The whole case is about the same size as the one I use for my Sony WH-1000XM4 headphones, which puts into perspective just how portable this setup is compared to a full headset like the Galaxy XR. You also get comfort and fit accessories (including interchangeable nose pads), plus a charging cable for the puck. Unfortunately, XREAL doesn’t include a wall power brick in the box.

C. Scott Brown / Android Authority

Getting started is refreshingly simple. First, hold down the puck’s power button (which thoughtfully doubles as a fingerprint scanner for unlocking Android XR and securely signing into apps), plug the included cable into the glasses-labeled USB-C port, and connect the other end to the stem of the glasses. On the glasses themselves, you’ll find a home button that jumps back to the Android app launcher, volume buttons, and a red button that cycles through five electrochromic dimming levels — letting you either see the real world clearly or block out as much ambient light as possible. I finally switched from Google Authenticator to Ente Auth, and I wish I'd done it sooner

A free service doesn't have to come with compromises.

•

Nov 28, 2026 — 6:00 AM ET

•

•

Yash Wate / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

Google Authenticator has been my 2FA app for more than half a decade. I picked it over others because it was one of the most popular authenticator apps at the time. However, 2FA apps have come a long way since.

I tried a few popular ones for a story a while back and, by the end of the exercise, was upset with Google for not keeping up with the competition. At a time when apps like Proton Authenticator, 2FAS, and Ente Auth come with true end-to-end encryption and plenty of practical features, Google Authenticator still feels like a decade-old app.

I realized I was missing out on a lot, so I pitted all three apps against each other to find a Google Authenticator alternative that fits my needs. Ente Auth came out as the true winner. I’ve switched to it since, and I wish I’d done it sooner. Here’s why.

Readers' poll

Do you use Google Authenticator?

0 votes

True end-to-end encryption

Yash Wate / Android Authority

A major difference between Ente Auth and Google Authenticator is how they store your 2FA secret — the key shared between a website or service and your device to generate one-time codes. As of writing this, Google Authenticator doesn’t offer true end-to-end encryption (E2EE). It only encrypts your codes in transit (moving between your device and Google’s servers) and on its servers, while retaining the decryption keys. Since Google has the decryption keys, it can technically access, expose, or grant access to your 2FA secrets upon legal requests.

On the other hand, Ente Auth uses a zero-knowledge architecture. This means your 2FA codes are end-to-end encrypted before they leave your device, and only you have the decryption keys. As such, neither Ente nor a hacker with access to Ente’s servers can read your codes. On top of that, Ente Auth is fully open-source. As a result, anyone can audit its source code to verify its encryption and other security claims. In fact, Ente Auth undergoes periodic independent third-party audits.

No single point of failure

Yash Wate / Android Authority

You can use Google Authenticator without an account, but like many people, I signed in with my primary Google account to sync my codes. Not only does that eliminate the need to set up a new account, but it also prevents you from getting locked out of your 2FA codes if you lose your phone. Just log in to the app on a new device with the same account, and you’ll see all your codes.

That said, this convenience also increases the attack surface — the number of ways an attacker can access your 2FA codes. Since Google Authenticator sync isn’t end-to-end encrypted, if someone gains access to your Google account, they get all your 2FA codes too. If they have or get passwords for your other online accounts, it could be a recipe for disaster. The situation gets worse if you store passwords in Google Password Manager.

This won’t happen with Ente Auth. Even if the email account tied to your Ente account gets compromised, an attacker can’t simply access Ente Auth and view your 2FA codes. Because Ente Auth uses zero-knowledge, end-to-end encryption, they’d also need your Ente Auth password to decrypt the 2FA secret and access your 2FA codes. So unless that gets compromised, your codes remain safe.

Cross-platform access

Yash Wate / Android Authority

Currently, Google Authenticator is only available on mobile (Android and iPhone). It doesn’t have desktop apps or a web version. I’ve found the lack of desktop apps to be a huge inconvenience at times, because when I’m logging in to an account on my Mac and need to enter the 2FA code, I have to pull out my phone, open the Google Authenticator app, then see the code and type it on my Mac manually.

Switching to Ente Auth has eliminated this hassle. Now, whenever I need to authenticate a login on an app or website with a 2FA code, I can simply open the Ente Auth app, find the code, and click it. Ente Auth will copy the code to my clipboard. I can then paste the code on the Mac and authenticate myself without touching my phone. Alternatively, I can access Ente Auth via its menu bar app, which is more accessible. The menu bar version is essentially a compact version of the app that lives in the menu bar and gives access to tags, search, and many other features you see on the standard version.

Quality-of-life features

Yash Wate / Android Authority

Finally, I like that Ente Auth packs a ton of quality-of-life features that simplify various everyday operations. For example, the app offers tags, which are a great way to group and find similar types of 2FA codes. I have a tag called work that’s linked to all my work accounts. This way, I don’t have to scroll through the entire list or use the search to find a 2FA code. The ability to find duplicate codes is another useful feature, and it helped me get rid of a bunch of duplicate codes when I switched over from Google Authenticator. The feature automatically scans and identifies all duplicate 2FA codes in your list, so you can delete them easily. I also like the pinning feature, which lets me pin my frequently needed accounts to the top for easy access.

Another handy feature in Ente Auth is called minimize app on copy. Enabling the feature automatically minimizes the app as soon as you copy a 2FA code, taking you right back to the screen previously in focus so you can paste the code instantly. I’m also a fan of the next-code preview feature, which displays the next code before the current one expires. So, if I open Ente Auth and the current code is about to expire in the next 2-3 seconds, I don’t have to rush to copy or type it in. Nor do I have to wait for the countdown to finish. Since the upcoming code is already previewed, I can use it instead.

Not having to wait for the 30-second timer to reset before the next code appears is a huge time-saver.

Among other things, Ente Auth supports bulk operations, unlike Google Authenticator. I find it really useful for adding tags to multiple accounts or pinning multiple accounts at once. The app also lets me add notes to my accounts, which is handy for storing the single-use backup codes that many services offer when you enable 2FA. Last but not least, Ente Auth provides a secure way to share codes with others without sharing your secret keys. Just select a duration for the shared link, and the app generates a time-limited link. Share it with the recipient, and they can then view the 2FA codes for the specified time.

Google Authenticator’s biggest pull has been that it’s completely free. Although that worked and gave it an edge in the early days of 2FA adoption, it’s no longer the case; Ente Auth does many things better and offers plenty of useful features, all while being completely free to use. I’m glad I switched, as I find the whole experience significantly better than what I had with Google Authenticator.

Finally, I like that Ente Auth packs a ton of quality-of-life features that simplify various everyday operations. For example, the app offers tags, which are a great way to group and find similar types of 2FA codes. I have a tag called work that’s linked to all my work accounts. This way, I don’t have to scroll through the entire list or use the search to find a 2FA code. The ability to find duplicate codes is another useful feature, and it helped me get rid of a bunch of duplicate codes when I switched over from Google Authenticator. The feature automatically scans and identifies all duplicate 2FA codes in your list, so you can delete them easily. I also like the pinning feature, which lets me pin my frequently needed accounts to the top for easy access.

Another handy feature in Ente Auth is called minimize app on copy. Enabling the feature automatically minimizes the app as soon as you copy a 2FA code, taking you right back to the screen previously in focus so you can paste the code instantly. I’m also a fan of the next-code preview feature, which displays the next code before the current one expires. So, if I open Ente Auth and the current code is about to expire in the next 2-3 seconds, I don’t have to rush to copy or type it in. Nor do I have to wait for the countdown to finish. Since the upcoming code is already previewed, I can use it instead.
Not having to wait for the 30-second timer to reset before the next code appears is a huge time-saver.

Among other things, Ente Auth supports bulk operations, unlike Google Authenticator. I find it really useful for adding tags to multiple accounts or pinning multiple accounts at once. The app also lets me add notes to my accounts, which is handy for storing the single-use backup codes that many services offer when you enable 2FA. Last but not least, Ente Auth provides a secure way to share codes with others without sharing your secret keys. Just select a duration for the shared link, and the app generates a time-limited link. Share it with the recipient, and they can then view the 2FA codes for the specified time.

Google Authenticator’s biggest pull has been that it’s completely free. Although that worked and gave it an edge in the early days of 2FA adoption, it’s no longer the case; Ente Auth does many things better and offers plenty of useful features, all while being completely free to use. I’m glad I switched, as I find the whole experience significantly better than what I had with Google Authenticator.

items.summary: This project might just be the cure for Googlebook envy.
items.body:

LineageOS 24 PC port brings Android 17 to your spare laptop

This project might just be the cure for Googlebook envy.

•

•

Mateus Seiboth

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Developer Mateus Seiboth has put together a port of LineageOS 24 for x86 PCs.

• The release can run of a USB stick, and supports systems with as little as 4GB of RAM.

• GPU support is a little more hit-and-miss, with AMD cards currently favored.

Android fans have a new device category to put on their holiday shopping lists this year, with Googlebook deals already arriving for Black Friday, but if you can’t afford to pick up some new hardware right now, we just found what might be the next best thing, courtesy of a project to bring LineageOS 24 to your existing PC.

It’s only been a little over a month now since we saw LineageOS get its big Android 17 update, and today we spotted a project that developer Mateus Seiboth is sharing over on Reddit: a version of LineageOS 24 for your x86 computer.

Mateus Seiboth

CapivaOS, or LineageOS 24.0 for x86_64 PCs, as it exists on GitHub, is still very much a work in progress, and Seiboth warns that there are plenty of issues and limitations, both known and unknown, but if you’ve been frustrated by the lack of good, modern Android ports for PC hardware, this could be right up your alley.

Specifically, it sounds like GPU support is still a little bit iffy, with newer Intel and AMD solutions supported, but NVIDIA cards or older Intel graphics potentially causing problems. The good news there is that you can easily try it out without making any permanent modifications to your system, and an ISO image available on SourceForge supports running live off removable media.

On the plus side, CPU support looks quite more robust, and the release even should run on systems with as little as 4GB of RAM — although 8GB is recommended.

Obviously, there’s a lot less polish here than you’ll see on a Googlebook, and you won’t find Google apps and services baked in across the platform by default. But if you’re just interested in “Android on a laptop” and aren’t looking to pick up new hardware dedicated to that experience, this sounds like it could at least be worth checking out.

In addition to porting the OS itself, Seiboth has also crafted a collection of basic apps that should make the platform feel a little more like a proper computer, including a text editor, file manager, and system resource viewer. Regular ARM apps are run through Google’s libndk_translation layer for x86 compatibility — there’s also Linux app support present, and that’s an active area for ongoing development.

If you’re curious enough to give it a try, let us know how the experience went for you (and share your hardware details) down in the comments.

Apple Store in Brisbane Reopening Next Month With New Design

Friday November 27, 2026 8:53 am PST by Joe Rossignol

Apple has announced that its retail store at the Westfield Chermside shopping mall in Chermside, a suburb of Brisbane, Australia, will be reopening on Friday, December 11 at 9 a.m. local time. The store has been temporarily closed for renovations since late April and will reopen with an updated design and the latest amenities, including a dedicated Apple Pickup station for online orders.

TCL's Note A1 NXTPAPER note-taking tablet is $150 off

TCL's paper-like Note A1 NXTPAPER tablet drops to a record-low $449.99, with a stylus and flip case included.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 11:50 AM ET

•

•

Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority

Preferred Source

Google Discover

Students, writers, and anyone who lives in meetings will appreciate a tablet that feels more like paper, and TCL’s Note A1 NXTPAPER just got a lot cheaper. It’s down to $449.99 on Amazon, which is $150 off its $599.99 list price and a new record low.

The TCL Note A1 NXTPAPER uses an 11.5-inch NXTPAPER Pure display with a matte, paper-like finish that’s designed to reduce glare and eye strain during long reading and writing sessions. Unlike E Ink note-takers, it’s a full-color 2.2K LCD with a smooth 120Hz refresh rate, so it also handles browsing and video well.

TCL includes a stylus and flip case in the box, so you’re ready to start taking notes right away. Built-in AI tools can transcribe recordings, summarize notes, and convert handwriting into text, which is handy for lectures and long meetings.

Inside is a MediaTek Helio G100 chip with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, plus an 8,000mAh battery. It’s also thin and light at 5.5mm and around 500g, so it’s easy to carry all day.

The deal is from a third-party seller, but the order ships from Amazon.

At $449.99, the TCL Note A1 is a compelling alternative to pricier note-taking tablets for anyone who wants a paper-like screen without giving up color.

items.title: Samsung is holding back these 30+ Galaxy AI features for the Galaxy S27
items.summary: One UI 9.5 beta code ties about three dozen features to a Galaxy AI version the Galaxy S26 doesn't have.
items.body:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Mobile

Samsung is holding back these 30+ Galaxy AI features for the Galaxy S27

One UI 9.5 beta code ties about three dozen features to a Galaxy AI version the Galaxy S26 doesn't have.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 11:26 AM ET

•

•

Pankil Shah / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Code in One UI 9.5 Beta 1 ties a long list of new Galaxy AI features to “Galaxy AI version 20271,” which Samsung’s own code labels as the S27’s AI version.

• Gated Galaxy S27 features span Gallery’s Recompose, new Camera ProScan and Log LUT tools, full-table AI select, expanded Scam Detection languages, and an Audio eraser for your calls.

• Several 20271 features, including Gen Video credits, Samsung Browser’s Ask anything, and Now Brief’s Bixby action card, appear tied to a paid Galaxy AI Premium tier.

• Samsung brought several S26 features to older phones this year, so not all of these may stay Galaxy S27-exclusive forever.

Over the past week, we’ve found dozens of new Galaxy AI features in One UI 9.5 Beta 1 for the Galaxy S26 Ultra, but many refuse to run on the device. When we dug into Samsung’s Scam Detection features for third-party calling apps, we noticed they check for something called “Galaxy AI version 20271,” a level our S26 Ultra doesn’t meet. Now, we’ve found code that spells out what that number means: It’s the Galaxy S27’s AI version. We’ve gone through code across numerous apps in the One UI 9.5 Beta 1 firmware on our Galaxy S26 Ultra, and here’s every Galaxy AI feature we’ve found so far that appears to be reserved for the Galaxy S27.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

Samsung’s code calls it the “S27” AI version

Every Galaxy phone with Galaxy AI carries an AI version number in its firmware, and Samsung’s apps check that number before switching features on. In One UI 9.5, two apps name the levels outright.

Voice Recorder labels 20261 as the S26’s version and 20271 as the S27’s:

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

Samsung’s One UI Home launcher does the same:

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

Our Galaxy S26 Ultra reports 20263, both on One UI 9 stable and on the One UI 9.5 beta. This is higher than the 20261 Samsung’s code assigns to the S26, suggesting the phone’s AI version may have already been raised once, likely with the One UI 9 update. Voice Recorder ties 20263 to “Q8_B8,” which, as we know from model number leaks, refers to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 that launched with One UI 9.

Every Galaxy AI feature we found tied to the S27

So what exactly is Samsung holding back for the S27? Here’s everything we found.

Gallery and Photo Editor

Several of the S27’s Gallery features have already surfaced. Recompose changes a photo’s camera angle with AI, and Shorts turns your photos into short videos. Both check for version 20271.

The same check also unlocks a few things we haven’t seen reported yet:

• Photo Assist prompt suggestions: The editor could suggest creative edits for the photo you have open.

Code

<string name="suggest_prompt_guided_tour_title">Get ready to be inspired</string>
<string name="suggest_prompt_guided_tour_body">AI will analyze your photo to suggest creative ways to transform it.</string>

• A new Restyle style pack: A download of new styles that only 20271 phones can get.

• A different Restyle image model: On 20271 phones, Photo Editor appears to switch Restyle’s image backend to one labeled “GPT,” instead of the “GEMPIX” backend used otherwise. The code doesn’t say which company’s model that is.

Gallery’s Gen Video feature, whose presets SammyGuru detailed through files shared by the Cipher Project, is switched off on every phone in this build. The code behind it in Photo Editor reveals more than the presets, though:

• A free-prompt mode, with “AI-generated ideas” if you’re stuck

• Videos of 3 to 10 seconds, in 9:16 or 16:9, at 360p, 720p (default), 1080p, or 4K

• Multiple photos as input, plus a sound toggle

• A watermark and content credentials on saved videos, and a cost of one credit per video

Code

<string name="gen_video_setting_detail">Transform still photos into dynamic videos with creative presets or AI-generated ideas.</string>
<string name="gen_video_max_images">You can add up to %1$d images.</string>
<string name="gen_video_credit_unit">1 credit</string>
<string name="gen_video_watermark_notice">When you save an image or video edited with AI, a watermark and content credentials are added to show that it contains AI-generated content.</string>

The same 20271 check also unlocks a Generate stickers button above cutouts in Gallery and other apps that let you lift subjects out of images, which sends your cutout to Samsung’s AI sticker tools. Samsung’s video editor gets a Creative studio tab for AI stickers behind the same check.

Camera

Stephen Radochia / Android Authority

We already covered two of the biggest camera features, Vision mode and Auto portrait, and both sit behind the 20271 check.

The Camera app gates a few more behind 20271:

• ProScan, which the Cipher Project spotted as an S27 feature, with code pointing to page flattening, two-page book scanning, and new PDF options

• Monitor view in Pro mode

• Dynamic frame in Shot suggestions, which suggests a better framing for your shot and guides you to it

Code

<string name="dynamic_frame_composition_tips">Tap the thumbnail to switch to the suggested framing and take a photo.</string>
<string name="dynamic_frame_target_reach_guide">Move the camera until the dot is inside the circle.</string>

Samsung’s Log video recording also gains two new LUTs, “Forest” and “Underwater,” behind the same check, which fits an earlier leak claiming the S27 Ultra will get an updated version of Samsung Log.

AI select and text extraction

Samsung Capture, which powers AI select, has a single 20271 switch that unlocks four features:

• Full table detection

• Two-finger scrolling while AI select is open

• An Add to Memory button, spotted by the Cipher Project, that saves your selection to Samsung’s upcoming Memory app

• Event extraction through Samsung’s private AI cloud, which we demoed earlier today

We managed to force the 20271 behavior on our S26 Ultra. With it on, AI select recognized an entire 83-row table on a webpage and offered a Copy table chip. With the phone’s default behavior, a similar selection on the same table produced only a “Translate” chip and a misread link chip (“Egy.pt”).

Separately, the “Extract text” tool in Camera, Gallery, and other Samsung apps gets Multi-select for picking several blocks of text at once, and a table view for tables it finds, again only on 20271 phones.

Now Brief

Now Brief, part of Samsung’s Smart suggestions app, holds back several new cards for 20271 phones:

• A Taboola-powered Top news card

• A Spotify card

• A birthday card

• A Galaxy Premium card

It could also use your YouTube interests and Bixby as new sources of personalization. The Premium card’s “Bixby action” pitch lines up with the paid features we’ve seen elsewhere. Internally, Samsung calls that card “premium_claw,” which suggests it could be how Galaxy Claw shows up in Now Brief for paying users.

Code

<string name="brief_settings_contents_news_top_news">Top news</string>
<string name="brief_settings_content_detail_music_and_podcasts">Spotify playlist recommendations for exercise, travel, and other activities</string>
<string name="brief_settings_contents_birthday_reminder">Birthday reminder</string>
<string name="custom_card_premium_claw">Bixby action</string>
<string name="custom_card_premium_claw_description">Automate tasks across your apps.</string>

Calls

Several call features we’ve already reported check for 20271:

• Fake call detection

• Recording calls in third-party apps

• Scam Detection for those apps

The same check also gates three things we haven’t seen reported yet:

• Google’s Scam Detection for calls, which launched on the Galaxy S26 only in US English, appears set to support five more languages on 20271 phones: English (UK and Australia), German, Spanish (Mexico), and French (France). Google already offers Scam Detection in those countries on Pixel 9 and newer phones.

• Your mic gets an Audio eraser option during calls.

• Call assist is turned on by default for VoIP apps.

Keyboard, Voice Recorder, and translation

• Samsung Keyboard: Refine voice input, which cleans up filler words in dictation, needs 20271.

• Voice Recorder and Samsung’s speech service: The apps can separate overlapping speakers, but only on 20271 phones. On those phones, Voice Recorder also appears to require cloud processing for summaries, asking you to turn off Process data only on device first.

• AI Vision: The app behind the camera’s live translation adds Google cloud translation only on 20271 phones, as we explained in today’s camera story.

Home screen and the rest

• Custom contact widget: Both the Galaxy AI setting and One UI Home’s “generative widget” need AI version 20271. It may be the same “My Custom Widget” that surfaced in an early One UI 9.5 build in August. Note that the launcher also hides the widget on desktops, tablets, DeX, and the main display of foldables, which rules it out on Samsung’s upcoming Android laptops.

• Status bar chips: SystemUI turns on new status bar “headline” chips, with “Next chip” and “Previous chip” controls, only on 20271 phones. This could be the centered, swipeable Live notifications chip found in early Galaxy S27 software that isn’t in the S26 beta.

• Audio eraser’s Now Nudge: It needs 20271 too.

• Smaller features gated by 20271: The same check also covers an animated effect for Now Bar automation cards, a weather card, and an “intent model” in the launcher. We couldn’t tie these to a visible feature yet.

Some of these Galaxy AI features could cost extra, even on the Galaxy S27

Stephen Radochia / Android Authority

Several 20271 features seem to be bundled within Galaxy AI Premium, the paid tier we first reported in early November, when the code hinted it could be limited to the S27:

• Gallery and Photo Editor: The Premium layer requires both Gen Video and AI version 20271, with “Upgrade your AI plan,” “Buy credit pack,” and “Higher usage limits” prompts.

Code

<string name="galaxy_premium_upgrade_title">Upgrade your AI plan</string>
<string name="galaxy_premium_buy_credit_pack">Buy credit pack</string>
<string name="galaxy_premium_item_higher_usage_limits_title">Higher usage limits</string>

• Samsung Browser: Ask AI (now called “Ask anything”) gets Galaxy Premium credits behind the same check.

Code

<string name="galaxy_premium_app_name">Galaxy Premium</string>
<string name="galaxy_premium_ask_upgrade_plan_title">Upgrade your AI plan</string>
<string name="galaxy_premium_ask_upgrade_message">You've used up all your free credits. Upgrade now to unlock more credits and advanced features.</string>

• Now Brief: The Premium card joins the extra custom cards for paying users.

Everything new in One UI 9.5 need not be S27-only

Not every unreleased feature in One UI 9.5 is tied to the S27 as of Beta 1. We could not find a 20271 check for these features in the current build:

• Zoom enhancer

• Samsung’s private AI cloud, SPAC

• Samsung Memory app

• Safe shipping

• Charging reminder

Leaked camera features such as Open Gate recording, Frame guides, and the redesigned Expert RAW don’t have the 20271 Galaxy AI version check, but that could also be because they aren’t Galaxy AI features. However, these could still depend on the Galaxy S27’s camera hardware and thus be exclusive.

Will the Galaxy S26 get these Galaxy AI features?

Brady Snyder / Android Authority

The chances for the Galaxy S26 getting these Galaxy AI features look slim, at least at first. To begin with, Samsung usually gates the stable release of a new One UI version to its brand-new flagships for a few months, while the now one-generation-old flagship is stuck with beta releases. So for the first few months of 2027, Galaxy S26 users shouldn’t hold their breath for these Galaxy AI features (and others that get discovered or announced eventually).

One UI 9.5 Beta 1 doesn’t show any way around that either. Every app we checked so far reads the AI version from the phone’s firmware, and we couldn’t find any simple way to raise it on the S26. For the S26 to unlock these features across the board, Samsung would need to ship new firmware that bumps up the Galaxy AI version, or update individual apps to lower their checks.

Paul Jones / Android Authority

That’s exactly what Samsung has done plenty of times before. The company eventually releases many of these “exclusive” software features to its older flagships. For instance, the Galaxy S25 picked up several Galaxy S26 features, including Call Screening, Creative studio, and the improved Audio eraser, with the stable One UI 8.5 update in May, a little over two months after the S26 launched. A similar update could bring some of the S27’s features to the S26 down the line.

However, note that several features need more than the Galaxy AI version number, such as new hardware or apps that aren’t on the S26 at all. For those, raising the version alone wouldn’t be enough.

Samsung said on its Q3 earnings call that it plans to bring richer agentic Galaxy AI experiences to its next devices, and One UI 9.5 Beta 1 code suggests many will start with the S27. The Galaxy S27 series is rumored to launch in January, so we may soon find out which of these features make the cut.

Samsung has not officially announced any of these features. We’ll keep you updated when we learn more.

Voice Recorder and Samsung’s speech service: The apps can separate overlapping speakers, but only on 20271 phones. On those phones, Voice Recorder also appears to require cloud processing for summaries, asking you to turn off Process data only on device first.
AI Vision: The app behind the camera’s live translation adds Google cloud translation only on 20271 phones, as we explained in today’s camera story.

blocks.text: Home screen and the rest

items: Custom contact widget: Both the Galaxy AI setting and One UI Home’s “generative widget” need AI version 20271. It may be the same “My Custom Widget” that surfaced in an early One UI 9.5 build in August. Note that the launcher also hides the widget on desktops, tablets, DeX, and the main display of foldables, which rules it out on Samsung’s upcoming Android laptops.

Status bar chips: SystemUI turns on new status bar “headline” chips, with “Next chip” and “Previous chip” controls, only on 20271 phones. This could be the centered, swipeable Live notifications chip found in early Galaxy S27 software that isn’t in the S26 beta.
Audio eraser’s Now Nudge: It needs 20271 too.

Smaller features gated by 20271: The same check also covers an animated effect for Now Bar automation cards, a weather card, and an “intent model” in the launcher. We couldn’t tie these to a visible feature yet.

blocks.text: Some of these Galaxy AI features could cost extra, even on the Galaxy S27

blocks.alt: Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra Galaxy AI

blocks.text: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority
Several 20271 features seem to be bundled within Galaxy AI Premium, the paid tier we first reported in early November, when the code hinted it could be limited to the S27:

items: Gallery and Photo Editor: The Premium layer requires both Gen Video and AI version 20271, with “Upgrade your AI plan,” “Buy credit pack,” and “Higher usage limits” prompts.

<string name="galaxy_premium_buy_credit_pack">Buy credit pack</string>
<string name="galaxy_premium_item_higher_usage_limits_title">Higher usage limits</string>

items: Samsung Browser: Ask AI (now called “Ask anything”) gets Galaxy Premium credits behind the same check.

blocks.text: Code

<string name="galaxy_premium_ask_upgrade_plan_title">Upgrade your AI plan</string>

items: Now Brief: The Premium card joins the extra custom cards for paying users.

blocks.text: Everything new in One UI 9.5 need not be S27-only
Not every unreleased feature in One UI 9.5 is tied to the S27 as of Beta 1. We could not find a 20271 check for these features in the current build:

items: Zoom enhancer
Samsung’s private AI cloud, SPAC
Samsung Memory app
Safe shipping
Charging reminder

blocks.text: Leaked camera features such as Open Gate recording, Frame guides, and the redesigned Expert RAW don’t have the 20271 Galaxy AI version check, but that could also be because they aren’t Galaxy AI features. However, these could still depend on the Galaxy S27’s camera hardware and thus be exclusive.
Will the Galaxy S26 get these Galaxy AI features?

blocks.alt: The back of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26 Ultra.

blocks.text: Brady Snyder / Android Authority

The chances for the Galaxy S26 getting these Galaxy AI features look slim, at least at first. To begin with, Samsung usually gates the stable release of a new One UI version to its brand-new flagships for a few months, while the now one-generation-old flagship is stuck with beta releases. So for the first few months of 2027, Galaxy S26 users shouldn’t hold their breath for these Galaxy AI features (and others that get discovered or announced eventually).

One UI 9.5 Beta 1 doesn’t show any way around that either. Every app we checked so far reads the AI version from the phone’s firmware, and we couldn’t find any simple way to raise it on the S26. For the S26 to unlock these features across the board, Samsung would need to ship new firmware that bumps up the Galaxy AI version, or update individual apps to lower their checks.

blocks.alt: Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra lay down next to S25 Ultra

blocks.text: Paul Jones / Android Authority

That’s exactly what Samsung has done plenty of times before. The company eventually releases many of these “exclusive” software features to its older flagships. For instance, the Galaxy S25 picked up several Galaxy S26 features, including Call Screening, Creative studio, and the improved Audio eraser, with the stable One UI 8.5 update in May, a little over two months after the S26 launched. A similar update could bring some of the S27’s features to the S26 down the line.
However, note that several features need more than the Galaxy AI version number, such as new hardware or apps that aren’t on the S26 at all. For those, raising the version alone wouldn’t be enough.

Samsung said on its Q3 earnings call that it plans to bring richer agentic Galaxy AI experiences to its next devices, and One UI 9.5 Beta 1 code suggests many will start with the S27. The Galaxy S27 series is rumored to launch in January, so we may soon find out which of these features make the cut.
Samsung has not officially announced any of these features. We’ll keep you updated when we learn more.

items.summary: Google is also working on a new AI Mode experience called ‘Ask Anything’ to answer questions about a collection.
items.body:

Google app’s Images tab may get a major redesign with more control over your feed

Google is also working on a new AI Mode experience called ‘Ask Anything’ to answer questions about a collection.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 11:17 AM ET

•

•

Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• The Google app is working on a revamp of the Images tab that brings some of its elements front and center.

• Additionally, we have discovered a new “Tune your feed” option to customize the images that appear on your feed.

• Google could also let users ask questions inside a specific collection with a new Ask Anything button.

It’s been over a year since the Google app rolled out the Pinterest-style Images tab, and it could soon get a makeover. For the uninitiated, the Images tab offers a feed of images based on your interests, letting you browse, search, or save items. Google is now testing a big redesign of this tab, along with a couple of new AI features for feed customization and collection-related queries.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

The existing Images tab includes a “For you” chip at the top, flanked by shortcuts to one of your existing collections and Saves. This Saves page includes tabs for All saved images and Collections. In version 17.78.14 of the Google app, we’ve activated a revamped Images tab, which brings all these elements together.

As you can see in the last screenshot above, All saved images and one of your collections appear as large cards at the top under a new “Curated by you” section. These cards show an image preview of the contents, along with the number of saved items. Meanwhile, the search bar at the top adds voice search and Google Lens shortcuts.

The customized feed appears under “More inspiration” and includes a new generative AI tool to customize what appears in your feed.

Tapping the pencil icon next to More inspiration triggers “Tune your feed,” which lets you nudge the feed to include specific types of images using natural language.

We tried to get the feed to show content from Android Authority, and to its credit, it refused the request and instead offered us the option to show general tech and Android-related images.

Lastly, the Google app is testing a prominent “Ask Anything” button inside a particular collection that opens an AI Mode conversation with that collection attached. From here, users should be able to ask a range of questions related to a specific collection, just as they would on AI Mode.

During our time with this feature, it accurately explained a collection’s contents, while also providing sources and other relevant information. This Ask Anything option could help users identify specific items in a collection and could be especially useful for people with several saved images.

Based on the extent of these changes, it’s clear that a fair amount of thought has gone into this redesign of the Images tab. That said, these early findings don’t necessarily mean Google will implement these changes, though we certainly wouldn’t mind seeing them in a future update.

items.body:

Google’s AI Mode could soon get a dedicated Library, pinned chats, and thread renaming

AI Mode could soon be much easier to navigate.

•

•

•

Joe Maring / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Google is preparing to add a dedicated Library section to AI Mode, giving users a central hub to access, share, and download their AI-generated content.

• AI Mode could also gain the ability to pin, unpin, and rename conversations, bringing its organizational tools closer to those of Gemini.

• We also spotted redesigned icons for the Google app’s Home, Search, and Images tabs. None of these changes are publicly available yet.

Google is preparing to give AI Mode some much-needed organizational tools, including a new library section to manage creations, the ability to pin and unpin conversations, the option to rename threads, and more. If these tools sound familiar, that’s because they are.

All the tools and functionality mentioned above are already an integral part of the Gemini experience, and it only makes sense for Google to port them over to AI Mode.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

We found hints about the aforementioned features making their way to AI Mode in version 17.78.14.sa.arm64 of the Google app, and although we had to manually enable them, there’s a good chance that these could soon make their way to more users. That’s mainly because Google doesn’t have to build the features from scratch — it just has to port them over.

We found the Library section to be fully functional after being enabled. If and when available, it will sit within the sidebar, right below the New thread button. Tapping it opens the full Library view with everything you’ve generated using AI Mode, with that specific account, on full display.

As seen in the screenshots above, you can scroll through the Library or long-tap a file to Share or Download it. Alternatively, short-tapping it offers a full-screen view.

The addition should make it easier to locate past creations, essentially eliminating the need to dig through old conversations.

Sneak peek: Google app is preparing a big change for its bottom bar

Related

Speaking of eliminating the need to dig through old threads, you should soon also be able to pin important conversations to the top of AI Mode’s thread history. We first spotted the functionality in early November, but we couldn’t enable it at the time. That’s no longer the case.

If and when available, pinning AI Mode conversations will work exactly as it does in Gemini. You simply long-tap a thread (or tap the three-dot icon on desktop) and hit Pin.

This moves the conversation to the top of the chat history, as seen in the screenshots above.

You’ll likely be able to have multiple pinned conversations, but you’ll only be able to pin them one by one.

Elsewhere, in case you want to search for conversations instead of always having them pinned at the top, you’ll soon also be able to rename conversations to something that’s easier to recall.

Gemini already lets users rename conversations by long-pressing a conversation and tapping Rename. The functionality appears to work in the same way in AI Mode.

Lastly, Google also appears to be testing new icons for the Home, Search, and Images tabs in the Google app’s bottom bar. At first glance, it’s clear that the redesign gives the active tab a slightly darker shade of blue.

The screenshot on the left highlights the bottom bar’s current look (barring the You tab), while the screenshot on the right shows what it could soon look like.

The redesigned icons for Home, Search, and Images each feature more rounded outlines. The Videos icon appears unchanged, while the Activity icon, as we’ve reported previously, will be replaced with a new You icon.

None of these changes are publicly available just yet. There’s no telling if or when these will make their way out.

We found the Library section to be fully functional after being enabled. If and when available, it will sit within the sidebar, right below the New thread button. Tapping it opens the full Library view with everything you’ve generated using AI Mode, with that specific account, on full display.
As seen in the screenshots above, you can scroll through the Library or long-tap a file to Share or Download it. Alternatively, short-tapping it offers a full-screen view.
The addition should make it easier to locate past creations, essentially eliminating the need to dig through old conversations.

blocks.text: Speaking of eliminating the need to dig through old threads, you should soon also be able to pin important conversations to the top of AI Mode’s thread history. We first spotted the functionality in early November, but we couldn’t enable it at the time. That’s no longer the case.
If and when available, pinning AI Mode conversations will work exactly as it does in Gemini. You simply long-tap a thread (or tap the three-dot icon on desktop) and hit Pin.
This moves the conversation to the top of the chat history, as seen in the screenshots above.
You’ll likely be able to have multiple pinned conversations, but you’ll only be able to pin them one by one.
Elsewhere, in case you want to search for conversations instead of always having them pinned at the top, you’ll soon also be able to rename conversations to something that’s easier to recall.
Gemini already lets users rename conversations by long-pressing a conversation and tapping Rename. The functionality appears to work in the same way in AI Mode.

Lastly, Google also appears to be testing new icons for the Home, Search, and Images tabs in the Google app’s bottom bar. At first glance, it’s clear that the redesign gives the active tab a slightly darker shade of blue.
The screenshot on the left highlights the bottom bar’s current look (barring the You tab), while the screenshot on the right shows what it could soon look like.

The redesigned icons for Home, Search, and Images each feature more rounded outlines. The Videos icon appears unchanged, while the Activity icon, as we’ve reported previously, will be replaced with a new You icon.
None of these changes are publicly available just yet. There’s no telling if or when these will make their way out.

items.title: GTA VI Now (Barely) Running on Apple Silicon Macs
items.summary: "Grand Theft Auto VI" can theoretically now run on Apple silicon Macs via unofficial community projects, despite Rockstar Games offering no official Mac version. Developers have adapted the Xbox Series version of the game to work on macOS unofficially, with some reporting that they can explore scene…
items.body: "Grand Theft Auto VI" can theoretically now run on Apple silicon Macs via unofficial community projects, despite Rockstar Games offering no official Mac version. Developers have adapted the Xbox Series version of the game to work on macOS unofficially, with some reporting that they can explore scenes and control the camera. Unfortunately, the projects remain experimental and performance is too slow for normal play. Mac owners can already play GTA VI through Remote Play from a compatible console. These unofficial projects instead run the game locally on the Mac itself. One project, " Halfwave ," reports around 3 frames per second in a prison scene and almost 5 frames per second during a boat sequence on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro with 48GB of memory. A separate test with 1080p output reached 6 frames per second in the boat scene. The developer also says saved games and free roam work, although lighting errors, flickering objects, and slow-loading scenery remain. Halfwave builds on " VIctory-macOS ," another community effort to run the game on Apple's chips. A tester using an M2 Pro Mac reported reaching the opening movement tutorial and controlling the camera, but at approximately one frame every two seconds. The projects use several translation tools as a workaround to make the Xbox game work on a Mac. Rosetta 2 handles processor instructions, CrossOver Wine provides Windows compatibility, and Apple's D3DMetal translates graphics into a format the Mac can display. AI tools are also helping with the projects. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, is already targeting efforts to bring the game to other platforms unofficially. A copyright complaint published by GitHub alleged that a similar project called "Leonida" infringed Take-Two's rights. GTA VI launched on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and Series S. items.summary: Taking off a protective case shouldn't double as a teardown.
items.body:

PSA: Amazon's 2026 Kindle back panels are popping off when owners remove their cases

Taking off a protective case shouldn't double as a teardown.

TL;DR

• The removable back panels on the 2026 Kindle and Kindle Paperwhite can accidentally detach when removing a protective case.

• The issue occurs even with Amazon’s official cover, but hasn’t been observed on the aluminum Kindle or Paperwhite Signature Edition.

• Amazon says owners can simply press the panel back into place, although reassembly can cause alignment issues.

We got our first hint that Amazon was preparing to make Kindle batteries easier to replace back in May, and the company delivered on that front with the launch of its redesigned Kindle lineup in October. It’s a welcome change for devices that people often keep for years, but some owners of the 2026 Kindle and Kindle Paperwhite are discovering that the removable back panel can come loose long before it’s time for a new battery.

A Kindle owner on Reddit demonstrated how their Ube Kindle comes apart when removing a protective case. TikTok creator Jackie’s Book Tally shared a similar experience, showing how trying to peel away a clear case to put some stickers on the back of her Kindle causes the device’s housing to separate.

It’s not just third-party cases, either. Mashable repeatedly encountered the same issue when removing the basic Kindle from Amazon’s official fabric cover. The publication also heard from a reader whose 2026 Kindle Paperwhite’s back panel came off completely when removing its case. The reader ended up returning the device in favor of the 2024 Paperwhite Signature Edition.

So far, reports have been limited to the standard Kindle and Kindle Paperwhite. As TechRadar‘s testing revealed, the aluminum Kindle uses two small screws near the USB-C port to secure its housing, unlike the snap-on design of its plastic counterpart.

Responding to Mashable, an Amazon spokesperson explained:

Your Kindle is designed to open along the edge of the display in order to replace the battery. If the back panel shifts when you remove a case or cover, press it firmly back into place on all four corners and along the edges, and keep reading.

While the panel is easy to snap back into place and the separation doesn’t seem to affect the Kindle’s operation, there’s a visible gap around the screen. The good news is that addressing this issue may not necessarily require sacrificing the convenience of a removable back panel. Amazon could potentially redesign its cases to make removing the Kindle easier without compromising how securely they hold it.

User-replaceable batteries are a big win for Kindle owners, particularly given how many years an e-reader can otherwise remain useful. Hopefully, Amazon can strike a better balance between making its Kindles easy to open for repairs and keeping them securely assembled during everyday use.

Apple TV's 'Carême' Wins International Emmy for Best Drama

Friday November 27, 2026 6:30 am PST by Hartley Charlton

Apple TV's French-language drama "Carême" won the Drama Series award at the 54th International Emmy Awards earlier thsi weekthis, marking Apple's second win in the category following "Drops of God" in 2024. The series follows a chef whose culinary ambitions draw him into espionage in Napoleon's France. The first season is available to stream on Apple TV. A second season is currently in production.
